entries.title: ‘Sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand’: Édouard Louis on 10 reasons to love Anne Carson
entries.summary: The French author discovered Carson on a bus while stranded in a snowstorm and has been enthralled by her fearless imagination ever sinceWhere to start with Anne Carson‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson1. Anne Carson is one of the greatest writers of our time. I discovered her work on a Peter Pan bus from New York to New England. I’d bought Antigonick
entries.content:
1. Anne Carson is one of the greatest writers of our time. I discovered her work on a Peter Pan bus from New York to New England. I’d bought Antigonick in a bookstore a few days earlier, almost randomly. From the very first lines, I was enthralled. While we were on the bus, a snowstorm suddenly blanketed the roads, and the other passengers and I found ourselves stuck for 10 hours in rural America, surrounded by an entirely white landscape. I took my computer out of my backpack and started to translate Antigonick into French. Spontaneously. I was so absorbed by the power of Carson’s text that I didn’t notice the hours pass.

2. One of Carson’s greatest strengths is that, unlike so many other contemporary writers, she doesn’t try to “make literature”. She writes. Sometimes clouds do the speaking, in her work, and sometimes monsters do; sometimes, in the middle of a collection of poems, she lets an imaginary Catherine Deneuve take over the narration. Sometimes she writes a letter to her own sleep and sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand. She writes about Homer, but also Rosalía; about Brecht, but also Marilyn Monroe.

3. In Carson’s work, time is upside down – out of joint, as Shakespeare writes in Hamlet. This is one of the strangest aspects of her work and it has fascinated me from my first reading. In her rewriting of Antigone, in the first scene, Antigone and her sister Ismene talk about Hegel. And yet, in Carson’s play, the conversation happens as if entirely normal, as if the ancient Greek Antigone and Ismene really had discussed Hegel together. One day, my friend Ivo van Hove decided to put on Sophocles’ Antigone and called Carson to ask her if she would do a new translation. Carson responded, “I already did a translation, titled Antigonick.” Ivo said, “Of course, but that’s not a literal translation of Sophocles – in the first scene, the two sisters talk about Hegel.” Carson responded, “That’s what’s written in Sophocles’ text. All I did was translate.”

4. One of Carson’s most wrenching texts is called Nox. In it, she tells the story of her brother, or rather, the story of her brother’s absence. When he was very young, her brother was convicted by a Canadian court. Rather than go to prison, he fled. He hid in Europe and Asia for decades under false identities. During the time of his disappearance, he would sometimes send his family a brief letter, or a postcard with quick phrases scribbled on the back. On a few occasions he called, just for a few minutes. One day, the Carson family received a call informing them of his death in Copenhagen. Carson gathered the photos she had of this brother who had just died and whom she hardly knew, and also the letters he had sent her, and she wrote fragments about her memories of him interspersed with an analysis of a poem by Catullus. She added in reflections on Herodotus and history, and very personal notes on pain and loss, reminiscent of Barthes’s Mourning Diary. Then she put all these notes into a box. And later Nox was published in the form of this box, with a single sheet of paper folded accordion-style inside bearing all the notes and images and fragments that she had accumulated. Never had a book looked like this – a shoebox with an enormous accordion foldout inside.

5. Carson thus spurns the limits of what a book is; her work Float is made up of several booklets on different subjects gathered together in a plastic envelope. Nox is indeed a box. H of H Playbook is a wide rectangular facsimile edition, impossible to put on a bookshelf. Lots of writers across history have tried to reinvent writing. Very few of them have also had the idea of reinventing what a book is, or transforming the book-object itself. Anne Carson did.

6. But Carson’s formal inventiveness should not lead us to forget the powerfully political dimension of her work. In Autobiography of Red, she takes inspiration from the ancient poet Stesichorus to tell the story of the monster killed by Hercules during his 12 labours. She chooses to tell the story of the monster, the victim, rather than repeat the tale of the hero, the executioner. She imagines a story in which a young Hercules and Geryon have a devastating homosexual affair. In her books, Carson often places herself in the position of the defeated.

7. For a long time she identified with Oscar Wilde, to the point of having a Wilde outfit that she regularly wore during her adolescence.

8. Women are also at the heart of her work, and always have been. In Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, one of her most beautiful texts, she makes Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy into one and the same character: two women who, despite the centuries between them, remain the object of the same masculine violence, the same dictates of obligatory beauty. Carson has also translated Sappho’s poems. And in her version of Euripides’s Bacchae, she gives an unheard-of psychological depth to the female characters.

9. On a more personal level, I can say that Carson has a distaste for the kind of social interaction that tends to come with a literary life. I sincerely believe that she likes nothing more than to be at home, writing. One day when we were signing copies of our books side by side, she said to me, “I really hate this!” Another time, after a performance we did together at the House of Literature in Oslo, she proposed that we quickly head for the restaurant in order to avoid the small talk.

10. Recently, we were talking about a trip I’m getting ready to take to Iceland, where she lives. I suggested to Anne that we do a performance together, with two voices, like we had done in the past. Then I felt bad about adding work to her life and so I sent her a follow-up message saying, “But we don’t have to do something public. We can just relax and enjoy ourselves.” Anne responded: “I prefer working. That way I don’t have to think about the world. Or myself.” How better to sum up the greatness of Anne Carson?

  • Translated by Josh Cohen

entries.title: AK Blakemore: ‘The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt was extremely silly and bad’
entries.summary: The poet and author on F Scott Fitzgerald’s perfect novel, losing faith in Ernest Hemingway – and the recent debut that blew her awayMy earliest reading memory Lynley Dodd’s Hairy Maclary from Donaldson’s Dairy – where an assortment of differently shaped dogs go on a walk – wormed its way into my subconscious when I was very young. The great dane (Hercules Morse, as big as a horse), the dalmatian
entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

Lynley Dodd’s Hairy Maclary from Donaldson’s Dairy – where an assortment of differently shaped dogs go on a walk – wormed its way into my subconscious when I was very young. The great dane (Hercules Morse, as big as a horse), the dalmatian (Bottomley Potts, covered in spots), the dachshund (Schnitzel Von Krumm with a very low tum) … I could probably still recite most of it from memory.

My favourite book growing up

I had a lot of picture books illustrated by the great Korky Paul, and remember being obsessed – even as quite a young child – with the intricate grotesquerie of it all. He’s probably best known these days for illustrating the Winnie the Witch books, but my favourite was The Rascally Cake by Jeanne Willis, in which a rotund, green-haired man called Rufus Skumskins O’Parsley makes a cake out of disgusting things (rotten eggs, spider legs, garden snails and so on), only for the cake to come to life and attempt to eat him. Probably more than a little bit of Skumskins found its way into the protagonist of my second novel, The Glutton.

The book that changed me as a teenager

I studied F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby for my English GCSE and it entirely reshaped my brain. I still think it’s about as near to perfect as it’s possible for a novel to be. All the stupid loveliness and yearning in the world, distilled down into image after image, with a core of white-hot rage, at the way extreme wealth enables – necessitates, really – extreme cruelty. There’s functional alcoholism, and then there’s whatever Fitzgerald was doing in 1923. Everyone should read it.

The writer who changed my mind

I had a baby in May, and in the first weeks post-partum I read Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience and Institution, by the poet and activist Adrienne Rich, while my son was napping on my belly. It made me realise that I’d wrongly – though, perhaps, understandably – held on to this notion that mothering would necessarily mean setting aside the work of the imagination, and a narrowing of my horizons, creatively. But Rich writes so thrillingly of parenthood as a politically radicalising and artistically activating experience. Rich’s work has made me excited for the years to come as a writer, as well as a mother. I wish I’d read her a long, long time ago.

The book that made me want to be a writer

Portrait of My Lover As a Horse by Selima Hill. I bought it with a book voucher in Foyles on Charing Cross Road, when I was about 14. I’d never heard of Hill, but I picked it up based on the strangeness of the title and cover. All of Hill’s poetry collections, as published by Bloodaxe, have this naive, under-designed quality to them. I read the whole collection front-to-back on the train home, and then again back-to-front. By the next day I was trying to emulate Hill’s guileless, cryptic style in my own – far less masterly – little poems. That was basically my apprenticeship as a poet.

The author I came back to

Jane Austen. Until my mid-20s I subscribed to that surprisingly common, reductive view of her as the author exclusively of novels about rich people having dinner at each other’s houses. But now I’m a rich person (in global terms, at least – I mean, I have Chanel foundation and a mortgage) who likes having dinner at other people’s houses, I’m like, this rules.

The book I reread

I often find myself revisiting bits of Virginia Woolf’s Orlando. In case you aren’t aware of it, it’s about a gender-swapping and functionally immortal Elizabethan nobleman who spends several languid centuries falling in and out of love and eventually achieving something like self-knowledge. Such a totally exhilarating, audaciously fun bit of work from an author who was – bless her – a bit of a Debbie Downer overall.

The book I could never read again

The Sun Also Rises. I was worryingly into Ernest Hemingway, for a teenage girl, whereas now I think he’s a bit of a pillock.

The book I discovered later in life

I’m 35 so I flatter myself nothing I could say really counts, but: I thought I’d use my maternity leave to finally give some Donna Tartt a go. I staggered through The Goldfinch and thought it was extremely silly and bad.

The book I am currently reading

I just finished What Am I, a Deer? by Polly Barton, and I was totally blown away by it. It’s about how we have fun and what we find funny, how we choose our friends and construct our pet fantasies, and I loved it, and I love how Barton’s brain works. She thinks so profoundly about the minutiae of modern life and modern social dynamics and I somehow found myself feeling strangely optimistic about the world and the eccentricities of the people in it. A banger.

entries.title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup
entries.summary: The Ballad of Black Tom by Victor LaValle; As You Wake, Break the Shell by Becky Chambers; The Eye of Goliath by Diego Muzzio; Our Cut of Salt by Deena HelmThe Ballad of Black Tom by Victor LaValle (Penguin, £9.99)This short novel won almost every genre award following its 2016 US publication. As a Black writer, LaValle had a conflicted relationship with the works of HP Lovecraft. As a child, he l
entries.content:
The Ballad of Black Tom by Victor LaValle (Penguin, £9.99)

This short novel won almost every genre award following its 2016 US publication. As a Black writer, LaValle had a conflicted relationship with the works of HP Lovecraft. As a child, he loved the tales of cosmic horror, but grew to recognise the racism and other prejudices of the author. Unable to “throw the man’s stories away” because of how formative they were on his own imagination, he decided to write his own response to one of the most obviously racist, The Horror at Red Hook, recasting it through the perspective of a musician and hustler from 1920s Harlem later known as Black Tom. It’s a powerful tale of horror – both everyday and the occult – told with sheer brilliance.

As You Wake, Break the Shell by Becky Chambers (Hodderscape, £22)

In this cosy science fiction love story set on a distant planet, life is a constant struggle for the human colonists. As the book opens, botanist Signy is yet to meet the love of her life, Cora, a rorqual pilot. Rorquals are gigantic interplanetary creatures, trained by human pilots whose implants allow them to communicate with the beasts as they transport supplies. Chapter 1 is followed by chapter 764, set more than a decade later, when the two women are blissfully married. The non-linear narrative may reflect what we’re told is the rorqual view of time, but it also removes much suspense. The characters are adorable, and the details of growing plants in an artificial environment, or Cora’s relationship with her rorqual, are enjoyable, but readers may grow impatient with the glacial pace and reiterations of their feelings for one another. Even the “naturally solitary” rorqual is given to declaring its love for Cora. In the final pages there’s a tonal shift that ends on a cliffhanger: how Cora and Signy survive is to be revealed in a sequel.

The Eye of Goliath by Diego Muzzio, translated by Rahul Bery (Pushkin, £12.99)

This first novel by an award-winning Argentinian writer is an old-fashioned tale of madness and the horrors of war. In an asylum on the outskirts of Edinburgh, circa 1920, Dr Pierce hopes to cure severely traumatised patients by hypnosis. All the men, including the doctor, carry wounds from the first world war. His latest case, David Bradley, was an engineer, but is now unable to do anything but desperately attempt to swim on dry land, until overcome by exhaustion. Bradley’s diary reveals the reason behind the man’s gradual descent into madness, as, cold and starving in an abandoned lighthouse, the rescue he expects keeps failing to arrive. Bradley’s own discovery of papers left behind by the last lighthouse keeper, a naturalist with a talent for taxidermy who murdered his family, adds another interlocking piece to this irresistible, haunting gothic horror.

Our Cut of Salt by Deena Helm (Orbit, £22)

In 2002, Marina is a young American of mixed heritage who takes a trip to Haifa, the city where her Palestinian grandmother Nuhad was born and lived as a child, until the family was driven out by the Israeli occupation in 1948. Nuhad never spoke about that terrible time, and now that she is dead, Marina wants to understand. When she finds her grandmother’s house, it is empty, for sale, and generally known to be haunted. Previous occupants have either vanished or died in mysterious circumstances. Entering, she feels anger, but then a flood of happy memories from Nuhad’s childhood. The house is more than simply haunted – it has become a vessel for vengeance, channelling death while longing for a return of the family it loved. The author allows the house to speak, which jars with the more realistic approach taken elsewhere. Despite a few missteps, this is a powerful, affecting novel about Palestinian loss and trauma.

entries.title: The Queerest of Folk by Russell T Davies review – the groundbreaking screenwriter tells it like it is
entries.summary: From Coronation Street to It’s a Sin, Davies’ memoir of a career in TV is also a rallying cry for creativityTelevision is an intimate art form, once beamed into living rooms, now on devices right in front of our faces. The screenwriter Russell T Davies understands that intimacy. Whether discussing his early days developing lost-to-history soap spin-offs, making a splash with the pioneering gay ser
entries.content:
Television is an intimate art form, once beamed into living rooms, now on devices right in front of our faces. The screenwriter Russell T Davies understands that intimacy. Whether discussing his early days developing lost-to-history soap spin-offs, making a splash with the pioneering gay series Queer As Folk, or reviving Doctor Who to great acclaim, he makes it feel as if you’re at the pub with him, settling in for the night, ready to hear his best stories.

This warm and gossipy autobiography offers a peek behind the curtains of the British TV industry, and as such, it goes light on Davies’s own life story. Instead, he gallops through five decades in the business, using the framework of his TV shows to propel the book forward at great speed. He was born in Swansea in 1963, to a family who loved watching TV. While he was studying English at Oxford, a friend suggested that, as he thought television was so great, he should consider doing it as his job.

That proved to be a lightbulb moment. Davies worked on children’s television, writing for puppets, before cutting his teeth at Granada Studios in Manchester, alongside Sally Wainwright, Paul Abbott and the great, late Kay Mellor. A little later, having created a period drama called The Grand, he found that viewers were turning off. Ladling on the misery with abuse, murder and a hanging obviously wasn’t working. There is another revelation: a friend tells him he is funny, so he should write like that. Afterwards, there is no stopping him.

Humour drives Queer As Folk, one of his defining creations. It is hard to overstate the impact of the Channel 4 show, which came out in 1999. Back then, queer stories were still vanishingly rare and largely miserable. Industry people dismissed the idea, assuming that a story about gay men would be earnest and dull. The arrival of this funny, Technicolor and defiantly explicit series changed all that. In one of many amusing asides, Davies notes that it was going to be called Queer As Fuck, until a publicist pointed out that it would never be discussed by Richard and Judy. “That was a red line for me,” he quips.

His other megahit was Doctor Who. He had written Doctor Who fandom into Queer As Folk, and when he revived the beloved sci-fi series in 2005 it appears to have been the fulfilment of a lifelong dream. His first Doctor was Christopher Eccleston, followed by David Tennant, and he returned after a long gap with Ncuti Gatwa, whose tenure was short-lived. Davies writes about it all with love, so anyone hoping for gossip will be disappointed. Even the collapse of a Disney deal and his second departure from the show are handled with grace.

Early in the book, Davies pre-empts criticism by writing that he is going to call a lot of people “lovely”. He does. He loves Abbott and Mellor. He loves Billie Piper and David Tennant. Producers, directors: many of them, too, are lovely, and he loves them. But neither does he mince words when he feels like it. Gwyneth Paltrow, who said that she would feel “stifled” by the use of intimacy coordinators for sex scenes, gets short shrift. “How remote and numbed and privileged you are,” he writes, scathingly. He recalls a money meeting with Harvey Weinstein, and how unsettling it was to notice the producer’s “baleful power”. He had tense discussions with the producers of A Very English Scandal, who lectured him on how to make high-end television. “But you’ve never made any!” he retorted, adding that “Old Etonians should never take on a Swansea comprehensive boy in a scrap.”

If, at times, Davies’ lightness of touch is tactful to the point of seeming coy, then elsewhere, his bluntness is bracing. His husband Andrew died of brain cancer in 2018, after eight years of illness. He writes about these years with a forceful and moving honesty. When people tell him that Andrew is looking down on him, he writes: “I always think, I fucking hope not!”

He ends it with a manifesto for the future: a rallying cry for invention and creativity, a call for hope and optimism in the face of ongoing threats to the arts from autocrats, AI and collapsing budgets. He cheers for the likes of Baby Reindeer and I May Destroy You, while also celebrating The Traitors and The Chase. If Davies has an ethos of television, then it is that there is no high or low. He is thrillingly democratic about it all, whether a straight-to-VHS Vegas-based Coronation Street special or It’s a Sin, his award-winning drama about the Aids epidemic. This is a warm and rousing tribute to British television.

entries.title: Agate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood review – a gem of a collection
entries.summary: Inspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimateIn the introduction to her first book of poetry in 12 years, Patricia Lockwood states that, “For almost a decade … I had not been able to hear it. The poems that I wrote would not end … too much was happening, there was a different kind of attention being pa
entries.content:
In the introduction to her first book of poetry in 12 years, Patricia Lockwood states that, “For almost a decade … I had not been able to hear it. The poems that I wrote would not end … too much was happening, there was a different kind of attention being paid.” It wasn’t that she didn’t want them to arrive. From Cave Painting: “And does she still write poems? / Not a whole one since I had been ill. / Five years. I kept saying I was / Doing it privately. So private even / I didn’t know about it.”

In that intervening period, Lockwood’s status has jumped from interesting US poet famous for the viral sensation Rape Joke to literary superstar: an acclaimed memoirist and novelist whose freewheeling, antic style is for many the internet’s maelstrom lassoed and put back on to the page. Who else can claim to have turned an audience with the pope into a biting comic essay?

So her return to poetry is a genuine event, and across Agate Head / Stone Soup there are countless moments that remind you that her poetic voice is unique: charming, whimsical, intimate; able to deliver images of great beauty, piercing philosophical insights and glimpses into a creative life behind the public persona. Readers of her memoir Priestdaddy will be pleased to see her father reappear in a few poems. “That my father has been drinking … / Always something new with him, / But I must say I didn’t see / 5-600 dollars’ worth of fine olive oil coming.”

Agate Head / Stone Soup is presented tête-bêche – head-to-tail in French, the volumes upside down and back-to-back. And while this might appear to be a frippery, the two collections have enough differences in texture to warrant it. Agate Head feels the more public-facing, while Stone Soup wrestles with more existential concerns, as beautifully rendered in Babies Born Remembering: “Screaming in the airport. / What do they remember – / Night flights, riding birds, / Being a set of wings / Themselves, a soul, an updraft.”

Both collections are inspired by stones, gems and metals of all shapes and sorts. Lockwood has been collecting fossils and minerals from an early age, and she and her husband have spent time learning metalsmithing, too. This gives her rich territories to explore. In Margaret De Patta, “Quartz wants / To be a window, wants a woman to appear. / We have properties, we are non-precious, / Wood horn bone and hair.” In An Agate a Day, we get to see her and her husband cutting agates, a hard stone with bands of different colours: “The trick is to hold the miracle steady. / We are the first to be seeing this. Ever. / Together. What happened to you? / We croon, after each cut.” It is notable that agates are associated with a sense of grounding and balance; an attempt to counteract all that other “attention”.

There is a detectable technical shift in Lockwood’s poems also. Many of the poems in 2014’s Motherland Fatherland Homelandsexuals featured long lines, allowed to run on and gather momentum to their epiphanies or punchlines. Here her lines are more staccato in feeling, jumpier in syntax, as in Not Seeing Glass Flowers: “To grow. Was it that / They looked real? I asked everyone. / Or was it something more? Max Beckmann’s painting is still a horror.”

It means a spikier initial impression for many of the poems. This ultimately works in their favour, as the thoughts accrete, moving in unlikely directions, before resolving into a revelation of some force. “Artists, no one really / Knows where they come from, / They fall a long way from the sky / And land zigzag” as Forged in Fire has it.

Neither collection is flawless. At one level, it is impossible to get away from the autobiographical detail, and so some of the poems become a form of higher gossip, our noses pressed up against the glass of fame. Sedarising, for example, comes across as smug rather than amusing.

And there are occasions when an object under discussion cannot bear the metaphorical weight being placed upon it. Polish Flint is an offender here: “The perfect ring I had married myself with / (Of Polish flint) was pried apart as I fell. / In slow motion, it seemed, surrounded / By tourists, with enough time to think / Of everything.”

But these are small bumps when time and again Lockwood leaves you with the distinct impression that she can magically make the profane into the profound, the holy into the hilarious, as she does to most brilliant effect in Monastery Icons: Windows into Heaven: “It’s sounding a little bit / Like you can order a whole husband / From this catalog, as long as his name is The Lord / And you are a PRAYING VIRGIN NIGHTLIGHT: / Just what we need in these challenging times.”

entries.title: Book of Lives by Margaret Atwood audiobook review – a dryly funny memoir
entries.summary: The Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and witMargaret Atwood had to be persuaded to write a memoir. The thought of writing about herself initially seemed “dead boring. Who wants to read about someone sitting at a desk messing up blank sheets of paper?” Yet, she continues, time passed and the possibility of a memoir
entries.content:
Margaret Atwood had to be persuaded to write a memoir. The thought of writing about herself initially seemed “dead boring. Who wants to read about someone sitting at a desk messing up blank sheets of paper?” Yet, she continues, time passed and the possibility of a memoir took on a “lurid phosphorescent glow. ‘Wasn’t there something appealing in the idea?’ my sinister alter ego whispered … I could thank my benefactors, reward my friends, trash my enemies and pay off scores long forgotten by everyone but me.”

Subtitled “A Memoir of Sorts”, Book of Lives is the Canadian author’s account of her loves, losses and literary achievements (she has written just over 50 books, including novels, short stories and poetry collections), and a fine showcase for her wisdom and wit. What little score-settling she includes is purely for the punchline. When a poet told Atwood in the early 1970s that she wrote like a man – he intended it as a compliment – she told him he forgot the punctuation. “What you meant was, ‘She writes. Like a man’.”

The book is read by the author, who is 86. Her narration is leisurely, gravelly, drily funny and unmistakeably Atwood. Though she admits she can’t recall much about her early books, she remembers enough about the important ones, most notably 1986’s The Handmaid’s Tale, her landmark novel set in a dystopian future. When she showed an early draft to the novelist Valerie Martin, Atwood said: “I think I’m gonna get into trouble.” Martin read it and told her: “I think you’re gonna make a lot of money.”

Available via Vintage Digital, 25hr 36min

Further listening

The Persian

David McCloskey, Swift Press Audio, 13hr 23min

This tense spy thriller from the CIA analyst turned author and podcaster sees Kamran, a Jewish Iranian dentist living in Sweden after being driven out of Iran, returning to his home country as a Mossad agent. Fajer Al-Kaisi is the narrator.

Elemental

Arthur Snell, Wildfire, 12hr 28min

Former diplomat Snell reads his compelling study of the huge geopolitical problems caused by the climate crisis – including mass migration, drought, rising sea levels and food and energy shortages – and how they can be addressed.

entries.title: Blockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge
entries.summary: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusadeDonald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American go
entries.content:
Donald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating.

It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave of explosive diarrhoea across the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. Cuts to tax collection also seem to have reduced revenue by multiple billions, though we cannot be sure of the causal relationship.

The other problem is that bureaucracies are hard to make interesting. Their work is technical and complicated, and most officials are taught to avoid saying anything engaging in public. By the time a journalist has explained what an agency does and why it is important, the reader may well have clicked on to the next thing.

So there are few better suited to the challenge of telling this story than Michael Lewis, one of the world’s bestselling nonfiction writers, who has a knack for finding an angle that cuts through the complexity. After a career spent getting readers excited about credit default swaps (The Big Short) and sabermetrics (Moneyball) he has decided to try to help people understand the importance of civil servants.

Blockers is a loose sequel to the The Fifth Risk, in which Lewis focused on the transition from the Obama to the Trump administration and the disruption caused by the new team’s almost complete lack of interest in their jobs. It focused heavily on what different departments and agencies do and why they matter. This time around the problem is not indifference but malicious intent to destroy. The “blockers” are the dedicated officials who try to stop the wanton and often illegal destruction of their life’s work by Elon Musk’s Doge or other agents of chaos. They range from a researcher working on preventing wildfires to a security guard trying to block Musk’s goons from entering his building, and a lawyer attempting to keep personal tax data from being used to deport undocumented migrants.

In truth, they don’t do much blocking – since they all either end up resigning when they’re asked to do something illegal, or are fired. The title refers more to the assumption by Musk and his fellow travellers that these are the people who are stopping progress and need removing. Much of the book is taken up with descriptions of the valuable work they did before being turfed out.

It would have been good to have a bit more on the villains, whose motivations for participating in Doge are varied. They range from the addled young coders with limited social skills deployed by Musk, to turncoat bureaucrats looking for any easy life, and some very strange characters such as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, with his bizarre obsession with dead animal parts. Trump’s absurd commerce secretary Howard Lutnick also makes a brief cameo, deciding he needs to personally sign off any cheque for more than $100,000. It feels as if there is more to say about the personal journeys that lead people to behave this way.

This is the particularly true of the boss baddie Russell Vought, the Republican operative central to developing the Project 2025 plans for Trump’s second term. Musk causes havoc, but quickly gets bored of Doge and heads back to Silicon Valley. Vought is the real deal, quietly and systematically deconstructing the state while keeping out of the spotlight and getting others to do his dirty work for him.

He appears in one of the book’s most engaging chapters, which zooms in on Francis Collins, a scientist who helped discover a successful treatment for cystic fibrosis, allowing those with the condition to live much longer. Collins ended up at the head of the National Institutes of Health under Obama, continued through Trump’s first term and part of Biden’s, before stepping down to run an NIH research lab. After Trump’s re-election he was effectively forced out, saying that his position had become “untenable”. Lewis runs through a series of possible culprits, of which Vought’s cost-cutting is one. What makes this particularly remarkable is that Vought’s own daughter has cystic fibrosis. Ideology is a powerful drug.

But perhaps the most interesting character of all is Sahil Lavingia. A successful software engineer, he bought into Musk’s vision and went to work for Doge in the Department of Veterans Affairs. He only lasted 55 days before giving an on-the-record interview in which he noted that “it’s kind of fine – because the government works. It’s not as inefficient as I was expecting, to be honest. I was hoping for more easy wins.” This was not on-message and he was shown the door.

A few months later, though, once Doge had fallen apart, he was invited back by one of the few survivors, who had stayed on at the Treasury department. Lavingia was tasked with improving the Internal Revenue Service’s computer systems, and despite not needing the money, seems genuinely committed to the task of making things work better. Through Lavingia, Lewis gives us a taste of what serious work to enhance the state might have looked like.

There are real problems with the way the government operates, both in the UK and the US, caused by poor resourcing, dysfunctional systems, or low pay for technical staff compared with the private sector. Alongside Lewis’s star civil servants, there are people who have checked out or become institutionalised. Lavingia’s lengthy battle to get a water cooler replaced reminded me of how difficult it was to get the lifts working when I was at the Department for Education.

One of the most irritating aspects of Doge’s brief existence was the stream of op-eds from people who really should have known better celebrating that someone was finally trying to enact reform, even if was being done in a clumsy and aggressive manner. In reality, Musk’s overweening arrogance, glibness and total lack of preparation have seriously harmed the case for proper reform. Not just due to the mess he and the likes of Vought caused, but also because they brought the very idea of making the state more efficient into disrepute.

Lewis is great at finding incredible civil servants and telling their stories. But agencies and departments should not have to rely on unsung heroes, battling failing systems, and doing 90-hour weeks for little money because of their intense devotion to public service. Most people employed by large organisations are not like that. Effective government needs processes that work when used by a regular person doing a nine-to-five job. Rather than trying to replicate the “blockers”, we need to understand what these superstars are doing and embed it in the fabric of our institutions.
